extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, workshop leaders and performers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for choosing, running, and teaching improvisation games (performance games, workshop exercises, dumb-but-fun amusements, and warm-ups). Includes per-game instructions, performance vs workshop suitability, variations, anti-patterns and running notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Games (category definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Games have something to teach you, promote good habits or sustain endless variety in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these games when you want learning outcomes, skill development, or sustainable variety. They are appropriate both for workshops (skill training) and sometimes performance, depending on the game's energy and audience attention span.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dumb But Fun (category definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dumb but Fun games are not actively destructive, and while they may not have much to do with the real business of improvising stories, they are not likely to insult the audience’s intelligence either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these for light entertainment and variety. They can be played occasionally in shows but are often more suited to relaxed performances or practice sessions. They are acceptable when you want low-risk audience enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never Play (category definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Never Play games are destructive or pointless or both, and survive on novelty value or because they crudely mimic some of the key mechanisms of theatre, or because they exist as a means for improvisers to show off how clever they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these for public performance; they tend to kill scenes, encourage gimmicks over story, or rely on tired tricks. They may have narrow pedagogical uses (e.g., highlighting problems) but should be used sparingly and with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm-up games (category definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of warm-up games for the beginning of a workshop or backstage pre-show to energize and prepare improvisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose warm-ups to loosen up participants, build focus/ensemble, break inhibitions, and prepare for work. Use age- and group-appropriate choices and avoid injury or embarrassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal Expert
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask the audience for an animal and a sport/hobby/activity; stage a television interview where one improviser is an 'expert' teaching the animal to do the activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid waffle—experts should not give bland backstory; instead answer with specific, absurd details that make the premise interesting (e.g., how the animal holds a cue). Do not invent properties that trivially solve the problem. Train experts to start answering immediately even if they don't fully understand the implications. In performance: follow a broad physical scene or use when audience wants jokes, but avoid when attention spans are short. In workshops: trains boldness, making assumptions, jumping and justifying, avoiding waffle. Variation: can interview anyone about anything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arms Through
rubrics_metrics.description: One person stands behind another and thrusts their arms forward; partner’s arms go behind their back so one actor controls gestures and the other dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arms character should avoid pantomiming every line but may make important offers; can be foregrounded by having arms give a lecture while manipulating mime objects. Best with two or three arms characters interacting; turning sideways wrecks the illusion. Props-heavy versions (table full of props or coat with pockets) are usually poor. Use judiciously; visual gag aspects must not overwhelm scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death In A Minute
rubrics_metrics.description: Two improvisers must complete a scene in sixty seconds, during which one must kill the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners often over-plan; best approach is a quick drop-dead early to force justification and story compression. In performance: useful in shows requiring 'challenge' elements (e.g., Theatresports), but not highly entertaining by itself. In workshops: excellent for 'unfreezing' planners and forcing decisiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dubbing
rubrics_metrics.description: Two players onstage have their voices dubbed by two offstage players who speak into mics; offstage players provide the dialogue for the onstage bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clarity, match gender pairs (boy dubs boy, girl dubs girl). Audience volunteers as bodies can work if treated respectfully. One dubber voicing several characters requires quickness and vocal versatility. Avoid four-way dubbing (A dubs B, B dubs C, C dubs D, D dubs A) unless you want chaos; four-way often becomes a train wreck but can teach failing with good nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fight For Your Number
rubrics_metrics.description: Four players roleplay a family and privately choose numbers 1, 2, or 3 with defined status behaviors: 1s are heads, 3s obey, 2s seek someone to look up to and boss others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Players must fight for their number; good for showing how status works and modeling families. Excellent for sustaining platforms but tends to inhibit character change; scenes may lack story. In performance: set up clearly and keep short. In workshops: good intro to status and can follow Status Parties exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finger Snaps (Master/Servant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Master has a servant who obeys a finger-snap; servant can perform any action on snap and master must justify it verbally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a blind-offer game requiring full mutual awareness. Servant should build offers upon offers, connecting earlier items (leash follows dog introduced earlier). Gradually escalate the absurdity to force the master to justify. Physicalization helps identify mime objects. In performance: good for director-driven shows (e.g., Micetro) and as a practiced procedure that can be dropped into other scenes. In workshops: excellent for making assumptions and practicing responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handbag
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrow an audience handbag; an improviser plays the owner, using items pulled from the bag to inspire character and justify actions in a seated scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask owner’s name and if they want to remove anything. Player should not act surprised by contents (it's their bag). The straight scene partner helps justify. Avoid cruelty to volunteers; don't overload scene by having both players use handbags. Works well for revealing 'in the moment' character and feels gently invasive for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hat Game
rubrics_metrics.description: Two players wear large floppy hats and try to snatch the other's hat; successful snatch ends the scene and wins; unsuccessful attempts count as losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This game foregrounds the 'second story' (a clear physical objective distracts from narrative). It's a perfect tie-breaker for competition shows. Keep stakes and duration short; don't conflate with other hat-stealing clown games. Be aware that the visible physical goal can override story possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: It's Tuesday
rubrics_metrics.description: One player makes a banal offer ('It's Tuesday'); the other picks an arbitrary strong emotion and overreacts, repeating the offer in that emotion and then justifying why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good for breaking down inhibitions about strong emotions and as an emergency tool to revive scenes. Typically not a performance piece except as a single kick to restart a moribund scene. Use sparingly in shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laugh And Leave
rubrics_metrics.description: Elimination game: any improviser who makes the audience laugh must immediately leave the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play when the audience is giggly; audiences told 'do not laugh' may perversely laugh more. Use on good nights; creates perverse incentives and is best done selectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master/Servant Double Header
rubrics_metrics.description: Two improvisers alternate playing two master/servant pairs, swapping roles so each plays Master A/Servant B and Master B/Servant A, enabling farce and transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests clarity of thinking and transformation skills. Nice to hide secrets and show double-crosses. Ideally show all possible combinations; servants behave differently depending on which master is present. Useful for farce structure and actor transformation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: No S (letter-ban games)
rubrics_metrics.description: Players must speak without using the letter 'S' (or another chosen consonant); using the banned letter results in leaving the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explores verbal risk-taking and good nature; S is a good choice because it removes common words but leaves dialogue possible. Players could avoid speaking and 'win' but that defeats entertainment value. Use as a tie-breaker in competitions. Variants: No T, No N, No I (ban 'I'). Avoid using rare letters or vowels which are too hard.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Removalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop game: players can blame each other for scenes going poorly; a finger-snap triggers two burly players to enter and drag the blamed improviser offstage, who protests the injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develops sensitivity to partner's wants and teaches when to abandon a scene. Teaches protest and resistance; can be used as a more subtle King Game variant. Use carefully to avoid real hostility or humiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexy Smelly Stupid
rubrics_metrics.description: Four players each privately choose which of the other three they find 'sexy', 'smelly', and 'stupid', then play a party scene where these qualities inform interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A platform-extender useful for avoiding over-introspective character work. Enforces transitions and gives players clear goals, producing funny scenes but weak narrative. Try other qualities (fragile, dangerous, funny, etc.). Not primarily a performance game but valuable for creating a rich world and teaching reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: An onstage player interacts with a tiny creature whose voice comes from offstage; onstage player must physicalize the animal and avoid looking to the offstage source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners often fail to name the creature; coax concreteness and purposeful character choices. Add quirky arbitrary details to the creature (e.g., transvestite worm) to force richer play. In performance: excellent story game that shows a new procedure; onstage player must know where the creature is and what it does. In workshops: strengthens narrative muscles, avoids wimping, creates purposeful characters, and practices playing resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak In One Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: A group stands tight and speaks dialogue in unison, each trying not to lead but to break deadlocks with noises or complete words together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often presented as expert game; tedious if expertise is supplied by audience. More fun with two creatures interacting or with audience participation en masse. Mistakes are part of fun; eye contact is unnecessary and can be distracting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed Dating
rubrics_metrics.description: Medium-form (~20 minutes) for teams of six-eight where each player gets an audience suggestion to inspire a character; pairs rotate through short scenes in a speed-dating structure to reveal changes across encounters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how characters change through interactions and builds anticipation in the audience as combinations repeat. Use to reveal character arcs and transformations; useful medium-form for performance when well executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twins
rubrics_metrics.description: Two players adopt the same bizarre characterization and act together (often repeating each other's lines) while a third plays the straight person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yoking players together bypasses the impulse to check impulses. Twins stick physically close, affirm each other's choices, and change together emotionally. Keep the straight person in trouble; avoid overlong runs — high-energy and short is best. Variations exist for how twins are created (mirror faces, audience suggestions). In workshops: releases bold offers and trains the 'Alice' straight-player response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typewriter
rubrics_metrics.description: One player is the 'typist' who narrates a story and pretends to type it; other improvisers jump up to play the characters, sharing control with the typist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginner typists tell overcomplicated tales; coach to establish a hero with a goal and to inflict suffering toward that goal. Typists should use mechanisms to move story on but not treat actors like mannequins. In performance: excellent sustained piece toward end of evening. In workshops: good practice for narrative skills, sharing control, and multi-person scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backwards Scene (Dumb But Fun)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a scene with lines spoken in reverse order (constructed from last line to first), or repeat lines in reverse order on a director's signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanically impressive if whole scene is reversed and can create clever blind offers and jokes, but emphasizes cleverness over story. Start with backwards TV interview (answer/question pattern) then progress to Murder In Reverse and open versions. Use to practice structure but avoid overuse in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clap Switcheroo
rubrics_metrics.description: Players clap to switch characters: when one player claps, everyone takes over someone else's character and assumes their position and characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be a story game if done well but carries a gimmick. Works best when characterizations are big and the scene restarts energetically. Not something to repeat often; requires high skill to avoid chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Da Doo Ron Ron
rubrics_metrics.description: An elimination singing game where improv players sustain verses to a pop-song refrain; when a player stumbles they are eliminated and a new rhyme name is taken from the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep group lines sung with gusto and roll to a new verse without pausing to maintain pressure. Preferred elimination game over 'Die' because it admits non-story fun. Practice group lines before using and avoid pretending it's a story game.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner Monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: Two improvisers play a scene while two others supply the inner thoughts of the onstage players intermittently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inner-thought players should provide counterpoint or contradiction to spoken dialogue; otherwise the device is pointless. Avoid piling on super-procedures (interpretive dances, over-elaborate accompaniments). Variation: letting actors speak their own inner thoughts is often as effective and less of a 'game.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel
rubrics_metrics.description: Three or four players form a panel on a suggested topic, moderated by a chairperson, holding forth in-character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tends toward jokes but is a safe TV-studio-like structure good for playing big characters and mixing groups. Use variations for character inspiration (audience words, costume pieces, identity cards). Avoid relying on celebrity impressions unless you have brilliant impressionists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pillars
rubrics_metrics.description: Two audience volunteers stand at side of stage and contribute one or two words to an improviser's dialogue when touched or when signaled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell volunteers to finish the improviser's sentences and provide words that are easy to drop in (missing single words). Improvisers must immediately repeat the volunteer word to make it audible to the rest of the audience and to integrate it. Use to involve audience while keeping control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound Effects (Dumb But Fun)
rubrics_metrics.description: One or two improvisers act a scene while another person makes live sound effects into a microphone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amusing and creates a playful give-and-take; not strictly improvisation but a pleasant audience interaction. Variation: have the audience make the effects for more involvement, though that reduces the challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thumbs Up/Thumbs Down (Yes/No/Maybe)
rubrics_metrics.description: A politician is interviewed and a spin doctor gives thumbs-up/thumbs-down/equivocation gestures to direct the politician's yes/no answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewer should ask clear yes/no questions and spot contradictions for justification. Variation: use a deck of pre-marked 'YES'/'NO'/'other' cards shuffled by audience to answer questions (stage as press conference). Good for press-conference formats and highlighting spin/doctrine conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Die (Never Play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Players line up and tell a story with the storyteller role moving on director's cue; faltering players are shouted out by audience 'Die!' and eliminated until a winner remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered clichéd and repetitive; creates low-interest content and encourages mediocre versions everywhere. Variants (suicide/eliminations, genre assignments) do not improve it. Prefer other elimination games like Da Doo Ron Ron, Laugh And Leave, or No S that admit their non-story nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrances And Exits (Never Play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each player has a trigger word which, if spoken by another player, causes them to enter or exit as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boring exercise in pimping that audiences tire of quickly; tends to feel like contrived manipulation and should be avoided in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freeze Tag (Never Play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two players start a scene until someone yells 'Freeze!' and replaces one of them, adopting the same posture to create a new tableau which becomes the new scene start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic workshop staple but criticized here for promoting cutting scenes off mid-resolution instead of finding endings. Tends to encourage tableau-based justification rather than emergent story; avoid in performance and use sparingly with clear purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre Rollercoaster and Emo variants (Never Play)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene switches genres (or emotions) over its lifetime; plot elements established should continue across genre changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although it seems to challenge continuity, it pressures improvisers to spoof genres and produce repeated gags; audiences often suggest the same genres leading to repetition. Emo variants enforce transitions but make everyone take the same emotion, which reduces one-person-change dynamics and encourages joining. Accent or genre-switch variants often degrade story and originality; avoid unless very short and exceptionally funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: MacGyver (Never Play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a life-or-death situation and three random objects, two players must concoct a solution using only those objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Painful unless executed with total commitment and lightning wit; even then often uninteresting. Possible constructive use: illustrates importance of commitment and clarity in crises. Avoid in performance unless players are extremely inventive and energetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign Language Translation (Never Play)
rubrics_metrics.description: One player is interviewed while a third provides (often visual-pun-filled) simultaneous sign-language translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriated sketch form with limited improv value; often works less well improvised than scripted. Avoid in improv shows unless extremely well-handled and respectful of sign language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superheroes (Never Play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a crisis, audience-named superheroes enter sequentially, each naming the next, and then peel off in reverse order ending the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temptation to pre-plan funny superhero names undermines improvisational possibilities. The strict order of entrance/exit pins improvisers down and can restrict imagination. Only salvageable with extraordinary energy, wit and commitment; otherwise avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibbity Bibbity Bop (Warm-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circle game where central player uses several moves (point and say 'Bibbity bibbity bop' or 'Bop') to get someone 'out', with many count-based physical configuration variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very engaging for children and groups; surprisingly effective warm-up. Use commonly known pattern variations (Elephant, James Bond, Monkeys) and adapt per group. Safe, energetic, and good for ice-breaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big Booty (Warm-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Group of ~5–10 with numbered players chants rhythm; Big Booty calls out 'Big booty number x' and the numbered player responds in rhythm; mistakes cause reordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good for rhythm, attention, and quick reaction training. Variations: replace numbers with words. Use for ensemble focus and fun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric Company (Warm-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Players stand in a circle; someone says a one-syllable word, next adds a word to form a two-word phrase which the group repeats; repeat with rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages quick-thinking, rhythm, and acceptance. Encourage low-confidence players to spit something out; group repetition validates offerings. Use rhythmic variations to up tempo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fling Shoo-ey (Warm-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Group stands in circle, removes one shoe, and gently tosses shoes to others with hands up establishing a throwing sequence; add more shoes as coordination grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fun coordination exercise; manage safety (no hurling heavy boots). Start with one shoe and progress slowly. Good for group focus and physical coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greetings (Warm-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants march and introduce themselves shaking hands, then repeat in different styles/moods (enthusiastic, funeral, distracted, flirtatious, bitter rivals, hyperactive children, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for mixed-background groups or corporate ice-breakers. Use style prompts to explore varied physical and vocal choices and to warm-up social imagination.
